           G-9 AND G-13 LANDOWNERS’ RESPONSE IN SUPPORT OF
           SAVE THE LAMPASAS’ APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13
       REGARDING DENIAL OF HEARING REQUEST ON ROUTE ADEQUACY

        The G-9 and G-13 Landowners1 file this Response in Support of Save the Lampasas’

Appeal of SOAH Order No. 13 Regarding Denial of Hearing Request on Route Adequacy filed on

May 18, 2026, and respectfully request that the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)

reverse SOAH Order No. 13 and require a route adequacy hearing be scheduled.

                                        I.     INTRODUCTION

        On May 6, 2026, Save the Lampasas, 4K Land and Cattle Company, and the Burnet County

Commissioners Court (collectively, Movants) filed Route Adequacy Challenges.2 G-9 and G-13

Landowners’ Motion in Support of Route Adequacy Challenges was filed on May 11, 2026.3



        1
          The G-9 and G-13 Landowners include Jeff Kubin acting in the interest of The Highgate West Group LLC
(d/b/a The Highgate Group LLC) (owners of tract 2141), Bob Guthrie acting in the interest of Guthrie Ranching LTD
(owners of tracts 2127 and 2128), and James Giddens acting in the interest of JKME Family Limited Partnership
(owners of tracts 2147 and 5142).
       2
          Route Adequacy Challenge (May 6, 2026); 4K Land & Cattle Company's Statement Challenging Route
Adequacy and Request for Hearing (May 6, 2026); BCCC Route Adequacy Challenge (May 6, 2026).
        3
            G-9 and G-13 Landowners' Motion in Support of Route Adequacy Challenges (May 11, 2026).


                                                       1
 Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation

(LCRA TSC) (collectively, Applicants) filed a Response to Route Adequacy Challenges on

May 13, 2026.4 SOAH Order No. 13, which denied the motions filed requesting a route adequacy

hearing and canceled the route adequacy hearing tentatively set for May 18, 2026, was issued on

May 15, 2026.5 As discussed in detail below, the decision of the Administrative Law Judges

(ALJs) to deny the Movants’ request for a route adequacy hearing was premature, based on

speculative assumptions, and would have a detrimental impact on the community.

         Save the Lampasas filed its Appeal of SOAH Order No. 13 on May 18, 2026.6 The G-9

and G-13 Landowners now file this Response to Save the Lampasas’ Appeal in support of the

Appeal and to further request the Commission reverse SOAH Order No. 13 and require a hearing

on route adequacy. Pursuant to 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 22.78, this responsive pleading is timely

filed.

         II.     ARGUMENT IN SUPPORT OF APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13

         The purpose of the route adequacy challenge is to allow intervenors the opportunity to

present a case demonstrating that the alternative routes the Applicants proposed were not adequate.

As the ALJs state “[t]he purpose of a preliminary route-adequacy hearing is to perform a more

cursory review of the application to determine whether it contains an adequate justification for the

routes selected and whether additional routes should be added at an early stage in the contested

case process.”7 The ALJs further note that the parties making the route adequacy challenge “must


       4
           Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation’s Consolidated
Response to Route Adequacy Challenges (May 13, 2026) (Applicants’ Consolidated Response).
         5
          SOAH Order No. 13 - Denying Motions for Route Adequacy Hearing and Canceling Route Adequacy
Hearing (May 15, 2026).
        6
           Appeal of SOAH Order No. 13 Regarding Denial of Hearing Request on Route Adequacy Challenge
(May 18, 2026).
         7
             SOAH Order No. 13 at 6.


                                                   2
 present evidence showing the inadequacy of an application or routes and presenting other superior

routes” and the applicants can rebut the challenge by “offering a reasoned justification as to why

any proposed alternative routes should not be included.”8

        Movants filed route adequacy challenges that demonstrated the inadequacy of the

applications and the routes presented by criticizing the narrow study area, illustrating where the

study area could have been expanded, and presenting multiple “corridors” that routes could have

followed.9 Movants provided sufficient evidence indicating that these corridors could be viable

options and have indicated that they are prepared to provide further information to demonstrate

alternative routes at the hearing on route adequacy. Nevertheless, the ALJs concluded that the

Applicants met their burden to show an adequate justification for the routes selected, and as a

result, denied the request for a route adequacy hearing.10

        The ALJs’ decision was premature and denied Movants the ability to provide

supplementary evidence as to how their proposed additional alternative routes or corridors could

be superior. Instead, the ALJs relied heavily on Applicants’ response where they broadly address

impacts that could likely happen as justification, but do not provide with certainty that these routes

or corridors cannot be used. This is seen in the ALJs’ reliance on Applicants’ response to Movants’

proposing to move routes further north.

        In Applicants’ response, Applicants suggest that they did not and cannot obtain federal

government approval in order to build transmission lines across Fort Hood and further note that




        8
             Id.at 7
       9
          Route Adequacy Challenge (May 6, 2026); 4K Land & Cattle Company's Statement Challenging Route
Adequacy and Request for Hearing (May 6, 2026); BCCC Route Adequacy Challenge (May 6, 2026).
        10
             SOAH Order No. 13 at 9.


                                                   3
 the proposed transmission lines raise “significant concerns” to agency personnel.11 The ALJs took

Applicants’ word for this in noting that the “[p]roject cannot cross Fort Hood without obtaining

prior federal government approval, which Applicants cannot obtain” and “[a]ny routes pushed

further north are likely to introduce military aviation conflicts . . . .”12 In making this conclusion,

the Applicants and ALJs cite to correspondence with various agency personnel. It is worth noting

that all of these communications discuss impacts that “may” occur; the Deputy Director of the

Military Aviation and Installation Assurance Siting Clearing House even states that “the DoD is

not bound by the conclusion arrived at under this informal review.”13 Thus, the assumption that

routes further north are not viable due to Fort Hood is speculative as it is based on impacts that

“may” happen. Additionally, there is land between the northern routes and Fort Hood that does

not include any proposed routes, and there is a transmission line in the area already. There are

similar instances in Order No. 13 and the Applicants’ response where the Applicants do not provide

justification other than potential impacts as explanations as to why these corridors are not viable.

        Thus, the question remains as to whether the Applicants’ alternative routes are adequate,

and whether there are alternative corridors or routes that could have been included. This is a

question that should be addressed at a route adequacy hearing. Requiring a challenging party to

essentially put forth its full case in proving the application is not adequate before the actual route

adequacy hearing shifts the burden from the Applicants to the challenging party to disprove the




        11
             Applicants’ Consolidated Response at 15.
        12
             SOAH Order No. 13 at 7
        13
            Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA TSC to Amend their Certificates
of Convenience and Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line
Project - Part 1, Attachment 1 – Bell County East – Big Hill Filing Environmental Assessment, Appendix A at A-
1022 (emphasis added).


                                                        4
 adequacy of the routes. The burden is on, and should remain on, the Applicants to establish that

the routes presented are adequate.14

          In denying the Movants’ request for hearing on route adequacy, the ALJs denied the

Movants the ability to adequately challenge the route adequacy at the hearing in which the purpose

is to perform a more cursory review of the application to determine whether it contains an adequate

justification for the routes selected and whether additional routes should be added at an early stage

in the contested case process. This is harmful to not only the Movants, but the Commission’s

review and eventual approval as the review is limited to a narrow study area. As discussed in the

G-9 and G-13 Landowners’ Motion in Support of the Route Adequacy Challenges, this limitation

on the study area and routes results in the unfair bias towards certain segments (i.e. links G51, G6,

and G44) and the segments that feed into them. A limited number of segments causes a particular

segment to be critical to most alternative routes, and as a result, the link may be selected not by

the required evaluation of factors laid out in the Public Utility Regulatory Act or Commission

Rules, but solely because that segment is relied upon by a disproportionate number of alternative

routes.        This is exactly what is occurring here and is directly caused by inadequate, non-

geographically diverse proposed routes.

          The impact of inadequate routes is detrimental to the community. As Applicants note, this

project spans approximately 200 miles east-to-west using 200 foot rights-of-way.15 These 200

miles run through the Hill Country of Texas and will not only take away from the beauty of the

Hill Country, but will also bisect countless landowners’ properties which have been in their




        14
           Application of Wood County Electric Cooperative, Inc. for a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for
a Proposed Transmission Line in Wood County, Texas, Docket No. 32070, Order on Appeal of Order No. 8 at 6
(Nov. 11, 2006).
          15
               Applicants’ Consolidated Response at 10.


                                                          5
 families for generations and many rely on for their livelihood. The impact is seen by the substantial

participation in this proceeding by many landowners. Not only have landowners been involved in

this proceeding, but several Texas Senators and Representatives have expressed their concerns

regarding route adequacy.16 As these transmission lines are a first of their kind in Texas and impact

the community so heavily, these proceedings should not be done in an expedited manner, and

instead should be evaluated efficiently and effectively. Part of this evaluation includes the

evaluation of the proposed routes and a determination as to whether they are geographically diverse

and adequate.

                                        III.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated above, G-9 and G-13 Landowners respectfully request that the

Commission reverse SOAH Order No. 13 and require a route adequacy hearing.
